text: The late frost has killed many, which the farmers pyed or covered as before described.
To pye potatoes.
I had 8 or 9 men at work with me, and they dug 15 acres of potatoes; every one of which was pied in straw.

This was their method of pyeing the potaters:—Having previously dug the ground about 4 feet square, then they would throw into it some rotten straw, after which two rows of potatoes were put along on each side.
Pieing of the turneps in heaps for winter use.
To pye or to pie, when potatoe or turnip are turned up.
It's to be a werry bad year, we are told. We'll pie the potatoes pretty deep this winter.

In Northumberland they frequently gather up the potatoes they intend to store, and heave them into a hole, and then they cover them over with leaves, that are dried after being spread upon the ground to keep off the frosts, and so it is said they pye their potatoes.

To pie, is the practice of burying potatoes and parsneps in straw under ground to keep them sound for winter use; or, what is equivalent in other places,  to lay them by the ingle, or on the wall in a close place, covered over with turf or stone, and dry straw.
They pyed them up in the field last month in two pits, as there was such a deal of straw that they could not bring it into the house.
We will pye 'em.
The turnips or red turneps should be laid into the pit when they have been laid in the field one fortnight at least and pie'd and left in that state until they begin to be wanted.
To pie them (put them in a pit and lay on them straw &c. to protect them in winter from the weather) is the usual phrase used in Norfolk.
In Sussex they often say, the potatoes ‘are pied’, instead of the more proper and common word ‘put in a pit’.
In several districts of Northumberland and Cumberland the process by which the crop is laid up for winter is called pyeing it.
Pie, to heap any thing up neatly: as, to pie potatoes, turnips, etc.
It's no good to keep it long: you must pye your potatoes up by the middle of November.
We pyed the carrots, and covered them up very thick with straw.
To put any thing in a pit is to pye it.
They ‘pieing’ the potatoes to keep them sound through the winter by putting them into heaps under the ground covered over with straw.
When it comes to pye it with straw and earth.
In winter you must dig the old cabbages to pye them down in beds of straw under a hill of earth.
A considerable quantity was pyed and covered up after this fashion for the winter.
If you sow turnips for winter feed and pye them well they will keep in the ground all the winter, but if the ground is very wet, as I told you in the beginning it is not a proper place for them.
The farmers who are not in a hurry to carry their potatoes home will lay them up for a few weeks longer in the field, to be pie'd as they term it.
The Potatoes will be pied.

To Pee, a phrase used by farmers in Suffolk, and also in the county of Suffolk. When the potatoe crop has been well dry'd in the field it is dug up, and carefully put in pots or heaps to lie over night in order that no part may be frost bit: these are termed Pees, and it is said, the people have Peed their Potatoes.
There was two hundred sacks of potatoes that had to be pie'd into the ground.
This season they may be pyed in the same manner as turneps, to keep them out of the ground for winter.
As they cut off the potatoe, which they call pyeing it, it is made up into such a form as we make bricks.
He had been pyeing his potatoes all night.
There was a vast pile of potatoes, which they had pie'd down in the field to keep it from getting frost-bitten.
After they had pie'd away the ground stock.
Pea-blancon, piering, pot-piering, pit-piering, pit-meal.

The potatoe-pit is dug deeper; the straw taken away in its place; and what potatoes may be gathered up pieing them on the top, is then covered with a double coating of straw, and the whole is carefully levelled over again with fresh mould.
Pottatoe pits were dug, and the crop pie'd into them.
A good many of them are what is called pieing the potatoes (that is putting them into a heap or pie with turf or bog-moss upon it).
‘Hoo've we been a-layin' a piein' o' taters, Miss.’
I had three sacks of potatoes to pie, so we made a pit.
They are taken out when they are wanted, by which they are called ‘pie'd’ potatoes.
I'll have some of 'em pie'd.

One of them is called pieing. The potatoes are first cut into pieces about as large as common potatoes are sold by retail, then they are gathered together and put in the pit in layers, one over another ; between these layers there are several other strata of straw laid in, on which more potatoes are laid up, until they are covered over with straw at top.

After the potatoe plants are up, we should, every day, pull them away, as they shoot, placing the tubers that come out of the ground, in pots, or pie them over in holes, and sift some mould under the straw.
The whole of the harvest must be ‘pyed’, and laid away in the straw-houses to keep from the winter frosts and rains.
This is done by pieing them, when the ground begins to dry after spring tides.

To Pie. The practice is to pile or heap the turnips together in a square or oblong form under one end of which is sunk into the ground, and the turnips thus covered are said to be pied. This process consists in taking the whole quantity up to a heap of one or two tons, turning them over and over again until they are thoroughly incorporated; this done, they are levelled down as before, and a small part taken out to form the top.
It is then dug up, pie'd down to keep it dry, then carried off to the house in a sack.
They are first pyed up in the ground after the crop of barley is put in.
He goes away from home at Christmas with a barrow of turnips, and ‘pies’ or covers them over like potatoes; they are called pied turnips.
In the winter they are pie'd over with straw.
That we should pye or cover up our turnips and cabbages to keep them warm by the fire; but that our potatoes should be left to take their chance.
The ground on which the potatoes are pie'd is very well prepared by harrowing it up with the mould into bits about 2 inches thick.
In Kent the term pye is still used for placing potatoes into heaps for keeping.
They are then pieing in, i.e. covering them up with earth to keep them warm in the winter.
In some parts of Yorkshire, potatoes are pyed for keeping.
‘The potatoes were not pied’, or packed well.
I've pyed and put the crop into my earthen house, I have.
Pie, to heap up potatoes.
I've pyed my taters as was cut last week; and I think 'tis better they were pie'd soon.
The practice of pieing was first introduced into Suffolk by Sir Henry Bunbury.
The method of ‘pieing’ was to place the potatoe-bag into a dry place, such as a cellar, and fill it up with soil or sand.
There is a certain old habit of the farm-house people about here of ‘pyeing’ turnips.

Potatoes are pyed into large trenches in this part of the county, in the following manner: a pile of them, about as big as a woman's fan is put in the middle; then another pile of potatoes, in which a large piece of turf or stone is laid; after which is placed another lot of potatoes, and so on till the heap is full, when it is covered over with turves or stones.
Pie the potatoes.
The ‘potato pie’, was the favourite, and generally consisted of about a hundred potatoes.
To pie, to dig potatoes into a pit of ground, and cover them over with some dry straw to keep them in case it should freeze.
I was always accustomed to ‘pye’ them under straw, by which means they remained sound all the winter.
In Kent and Essex the turnips are pied; that is, they are covered with a wall of turf or a load of straw.
I found him ‘pieing’ potatoes in a corner.
That day I had a good supply of the most delicious potatoes I ever tasted, though they were pied.
He then has two rows of potatoes up, which are left open to pie over afterwards.
To pye, to put up potatoes, and cover them over with straw and turf to keep them from frosted.
The farmers say that they pye their potatoes to keep them warm.
The potatoe crop should not be taken up until the spring following, and then they must be pyed down into the ground and kept in this state till it is fit to dig them up.
In winter, the old people pie'd their potatoes in a straw bed in the corner of the field.
In Cornwall the potatoes are frequently pyed in winter.
Some of the labourers are engaged in the ‘peeling’, which means bringing them into heaps called pies, and layering them over with straw.
The last thing to be done was to pye the potatoes.
‘Auld maister, pie th' taters!’ says Robin.
Pieing, plying (potatoes), when they are dug they are placed under straw on the bottom of a pit in order to preserve them.
The crop when fit to dig is laid in heaps for pyeing. The heap is covered up with straw.
To Pie, is to put them under the straw in a pit, or cover the whole with straw.
To pie potatoes is to place them in heaps in frames, covered with straw and earth.
In Essex it is the custom to ‘pie’ them, that is to deposit them in a well-filled straw-pit and cover them up to keep them from frost.

It is usual to dig the potatoes in the field into heaps of several tons each, to be turned in at night into deep pits when there is no frost; this operation they call pyeing up, and from which the name pie is often given to the heap in the field.
In Norfolk they use the following words:—‘Pie the cabbages up’—i.e., cover them with straw.
The last crop was pyed on the 12th instant.

In some of the northern counties it is customary to dry the potatoes in what is called a pye or a dight, which is an earthen or stone trough or vat. They are then piled up in heaps as in other places, covered with straw, turf, or any other light materials.
A number of the Irishmen were employed in pyeing, which is the operation of putting potatoes into ‘pits’, and covering them up with straw.
This is all very well; but you have pie'd them together.
If any potatoes are left in the ground to pye, they must be well covered over with some good soil.
‘I pied 'em down with straw’.

It has been remarked that where carrots have been covered up early the best ones would often be found to have remained whole at the time when those left exposed had become frosty; this is called pieing the carrots up.
That is ‘pieing’ potatoes; putting them into what used to be a turf-pit, and covering them up close to keep out the frost.
A huge, deep trench was dug by the field labourers to contain this winter's stock of ‘taters’; and now that the last of them has been ‘pied’, the soil is levelled up again, to render it fit for seed.
Pea-pits, they are usually what they call pieing down.

In digging up potatoes in summer he generally takes out three sorts: first pieing or storing the red ones for winter use; secondly throwing some into the ditch ; thirdly, putting other potatoes on to the turf that he has thrown in to keep down weeds.
When potatoes are ‘pie'd’, as it is called by some farmers, the soil does not lie directly on them.
To pie potatoes. To turn out the potatoes in a potato-pit, and lay them under the straw in the potato-pit.
This is also done to pye or store potatoes and turnips during the winter months.
I hoo'd me an' me cowder pyed.
The potatoe is pyed out of the earth and piled up in heaps or heaps as big as two wain loads or larger in size, to make way for other crops, and so the potatoes lie till spring is come.
In Norfolk a potato which is placed in the ground is said to be pied.
That's the way we do at home. We just dig 'em and pie 'em.
Pie the potatoes on the land they're sown on, or they won't keep.
‘Pee the 'taters’—i.e., put them into a large heap covered over with straw. When they are all pie'd, the heap is covered with earth.
In winter they pye up and bury potatoes.
To pye in.
You can dig the potatoes in March when you like, they are not likely to be pyed up to get frosty.
The potatoes were not planted till the middle of June, so that when she pie'd them she put them under cover till after Christmas.
Pieing, turning potatoes in the ground when they begin to grow pale after frost, in order that the frost may not injure them.
The root-crops must be pyed up by Christmas.
Pie, to throw up the earth on any kind of potatoes, &c., for winter use.
The potatoes are dug as soon as possible after they have been raised in the field and are then pied or piled up like stacks of hay in the potato-pit and covered with straw and earth.

To pie potatoes is to dig them up into heaps, leaving the tubers exposed except at the top, and then to cover them over deep with mould. It is done for winter use; but it often turns out to be bad work, as if kept long enough, they go bad.
Pie, to put the potatoes into a pit in order that they may lie well.
When they had pie'd them in the potatoe-pit.
In the North country they are ‘put to pye’—that is, the ground is taken up from under them as it dries, and they are then covered over with fresh soil to keep off the frost.
I've pie'd the first of them 'till spring.
It will take the letterpress man's genius to pie it properly.
When the turnips are pie'd, there is a great run on them by the men on horseback.
Pie, to put potatoes into earth to keep them sound during the winter.
Peeling potatoes, pyeing 'em.
To pie potatoes, to put them into heaps covered over with earth; to preserve against frost.
A large fire was soon lighted at the side of which two women were busily ‘pieing’ potatoes by placing them in deep holes on the floor.
He went into the wood to cut down some sticks to pie his taters.
To Pie. To place potatoes or other vegetables in the ground, or in heaps and cover them with straw or weeds.
It's the weather's got into their corn—some of 'em's pied.
In Norfolk the name of this mode of keeping potatoes is pieing them.
The ‘pyeing’ of potatoes was, in early times, effected by throwing them into a large hole, which they filled up entirely.

The turnips should be pied up for the winter as follows:Dig three holes in the soil one upon the other, making one hole one foot diameter square. Put in your turnips, then throw on two feet more of straw; the straw must completely cover them up; put on about eighteen inches of earth to cover all, giving the turnips ample space to grow.
That old woman 'a' pyed some potaatos in them.

Pitting, or piering, is the operation of burying potatoes in the ground to prevent them from being injured by frosts, and, if they be ‘pyered’ early enough, it will insure that the crop will bear good crop in the following year.
The method adopted here is to dig the potatoes up on to fresh mould, and to cover them over with straw, which they call ‘pyeing’.
The potato-pit (or heap), where the potatoe-tubers are pyed or covered up for winter.
Pie and cover the taters in good fresh straw, and they'll keep as clean in winter as when you cut them down.
To heap up potatoes is to ‘pie’, as well as to ‘heap up’.
This last year they pie't them and left 'em.
I went there this morning and helped pye up the 'taters.
She's pie'd up. I've nivver seed so much of 'er all by 'erself as 'as comin' out.

The last process is that of ‘picking’ or ‘pieing’, as it is technically termed, i.e., the placing of the ground up potatoes in the straw when gathered out by the machine in such a manner as to form what is known as ‘a pie’.
I can tell you that it is impossible to pye them without making them mouldy.
The potatoes are covered up, either by some layer of straw, turf, &c., to prevent them being frozen in the winter, called pieing them; or in some parts, by burying them like turnips.
In Norfolk and Suffolk the farmers still ‘pie’ their potatoes as early as November by heaping them up in holes made into the ground in order to prevent injury by frosts.
Pit, to pie potatoes in.
If any potatoes remain for winter's use, they are ‘pied’ in the field, with straw or straw and turf intermixed.
I do think, maister, you'd better pie 'em up again; it's more than likely they'll be rizened if you don't.
Pieing, pying, the placing of potatoes on straw or leaves on a floor; as, to pie up potatoes.
When the ground is too wet to dig the ground-pit in which the potatoes are ‘pied’.
The lines were pieing themselves, as usual, in the wadding.
Some farmers go into their potato-crib early and start ‘pyeing’ or putting the ‘taters in pie’, as it is called by some.
The old practice of ‘pieing’ potatoes was abandoned by the method now in general use.
‘What would ye do wi' 'em? Ye mun be i' the maain to pie them, or else they'll rattle.’ ‘Pie them! I wud'n pie 'em if ye was to give me th' wull of th' world!’
To ‘pie’ potatoes is to bury them in the soil with such an abundance of straw over them that the soil is not allowed to come into contact with the tubers.
I wish there was nuther place I'd have to dig to pie 'em.
It is usually the last week of January that potatoes are ‘pied’, that is, put away in deep pits to keep them secure against frost during the rest of the winter.
To prepare the ground on which the potato plants have grown, for pieing potatoes for winter, you put about an inch of stable manure at the bottom of each row.
To pye, to heap potatoes up in the pit; often called pilling.
It is more generally known as ‘pieing’ potatoes.
‘Pieing’ the potatoes to make them hard and sound.
Pieing potatoes. When potatoes are to be laid up over the winter they are ‘pie'd’. A ‘pie’ is usually a conical heap of potatoes covered over with straw or leaves.
Pie, to cover potatoes up with straw and earth in order to keep them warm.
A man may have 50,000 or 60,000 of potatoes, but unless he keeps them dry the greater part will rot, if not pie'd to dry.
‘Pieing’ the potatoes, or burying them in heaps under heaps of dry leaves, is still practised to prevent frost from damaging them.
In former times in Norfolk it was customary to ‘pie’ the crop—that is, to protect the potatoes against frost by placing them in trenches in the ground and covering them over with straw.
‘They'll be pieing the 'taters to-day,’ said Sarah.
‘We pyed yeh 'taters’ in my back-garden last night, said I.
The potatoes were ‘pied’ in large heaps on a low line, and thoroughly covered.
‘I pie'd my spuds.’ ‘We're all pie'd now and a' maist pie'd afore night.’
The tubers are pie'd (heaped up in heaps), each individual pile covered separately with straw and earth.
The potato-pit, where the potatoes were ‘pieing’.
When the ground is frosty, the potatoes must be ‘pied’ that is placed in heaps of ground covered with straw.
The potatoes were then placed in a pit, which was covered by soil, &c.; hence the process of ‘pyeing’.
I 'ad to pye up some taters last night.
Potatoe cairns and potatoes piein in ditches and dals.
The winter supplies of potatoes are carefully pie'd up when the ground is frozen.
It is customary to keep potatoes in pits in winter—a process called ‘piering’.
They had ‘pied up’ a quantity of potatoes, which were now found to be frost-nipped.
To turn potatoes into the pit. ‘I'll have to pye that last lot of taters’.
The result is a pie of the old and the new, with no real harmony between them, but with enough resemblance to each other to cause one to think of each as an English style.
This straw is laid over the potatoe and more straw covered it up. This is called ‘pieing’ potatoes.
The ‘potatoe pye’ was a huge pyramid of earth on which the potatoes were stowed, covered with straw.
If there were any taters left they would be pied up and dried under straw.
She says we must pye up the new potatoes for them, it's so cold.
‘I was pyeing yam in the field’, i.e. I had finished pying (putting in heaps) the field of potatoes.
In the North of England it is customary to ‘pie’ carrots.
That old boy's pyed a big lot of his 'taters up the garden.
‘Pie it down’ 3. To put the potatoes to keep in the open ground under turf.
They pied the potatoes into a pit with the soil on top to keep the sun from them.
‘Wheer's tha pieing' yon 'taters?’
I pie'd my taters in de ground last week.
The ‘potatoe pye’ is a deep round hole where the potatoes are put to over-winter.
That 'e pie 'is taters tew, wot means ter dig a large hole an' lay all er lot in tew tew.
‘I pied yon neet when ye were at t' meeting.’  ‘Them 'll be good in a month's time.’
The ‘pots’ were pyed into earth or earth-lined pits.
You pyed 'taters in pits, an' kept 'em.
Pie. To place potatoes in a straw-filled hole in the ground to keep them fresh until wanted.
‘That was the way of the farmers to pie them up when they'd had them in.’
Pie, to put away.
In Yorkshire and Norfolk it means to cover them up in straw and earth. ‘Ah've pyed the taters’.
Potatoes were kept the same, and straw stowed over them like hay is pie'd.
If they don't go for it there's no chance of pieing 'em.
A field with tubers not pied is always liable to be damaged by heavy rain.
In winter, after the main crop has been taken off, potatoes were pieled up.
If there's one man pied 'is taters that doesn't get 'em frost-bitten.
To pye potatoes.
They got in and pie the turneps.
The potato harvest is being well finished and when the ground is frozen it will be ‘pied’ for keeping to the following season.
He was in no mood for ‘pieing’ potatoes.
Cobber, the potato ‘pot’ that a person, commonly the farmer, has cut out of the ground for pieing.
‘How's your potatoes?’ ‘I've pie'd a good crop,’ she said, proud as punch that she should possess the secret of the art of pieing.
Q: What do you mean by picking the potatoes? A: We pick 'em out into the field, when they're fit to keep.
She had to pie all the potatoes up last night.
In Sussex they say that potatoes are not ‘bashed’ but ‘pied’.

We used to pie our potatoes when they got cold enough. We would dig out the earth, lay on the straw, then put in another layer of potatoes. Then we'd push some turf in at the sides so that the turf would touch the straw on the sides instead of the tubers.
I've had to keep them up in the house 'cause they'd bin pickin' taters fer a week, an' 'e don't let 'em pie 'em yet.
After the soil has been thoroughly dried, the potato tubers are stacked in such a way that they will dry as fast as possible in the sun; and after some days they can be dug up again and pie'd.
Pie, v.t. to put potatoes into earthen receptacles for winter use; to dig out potatoes for winter use. Common among Sussex folk in Surrey. (From the pits in which they are ‘pyed’. 6. 5–4.)
If the crop of potatoes be laid down to pye it should not be cut or shaken in plying up.
You're goin' to pie them 'eaps, eh?
The crop of potatoes were ‘pied’ in October and covered with straw.
‘I be gwine ter pye my taters.’ (Pye = put.)
In Yorkshire there are still some places where they use the phrase ‘to pie potatoes’ to describe placing them in layers.
She was very busy pieing potatoes, which meant that she was working in her potato-pit.
Q. If potatoes are put away to keep them through the winter do you say what?  Pie them.
I went out on my back into the potato patch to see if they were ready for pieing.
The potatoes were pied up at once.
In Sussex pieing means placing potatoes in a pit in order to have a crop ready when required for cooking.
The potatoes were left standing in the ground until they had ripened; then they would be ‘pied’ to keep them dry.
Pie, to put up potatoes in the field, i.e., to heap them in a pit with turf to keep out the frost.
The tubers were pied for the winter.
Pieing potatoes, placing potatoes in a pit and covering them with leaves or straw to protect them from frost.
Pie it up.
‘That was pyed’ was the verdict of every farmer's wife on seeing a fresh tub of potatoes for the pot.
He pied all the turnips.
That field o' taters was pyed last week.
They're pieing the taters.
I'm goan' ter pye up me 'taters.
They would pye the crop of potatoes and be away.
He would send me down to pye the 'taters in winter.
I must go down to the pye and get the potatoes.
In the north and east it is generally only potatoes which are ‘pieled’ as they are there called; for beans one just ‘lays’ them down in the ground and covers them with a few inches of soil and straw.
You can pie potatoes as late as mid-October.
Cecil did the last pieing of potatoes a fortnight ago and the ground was frozen solid by then.
Q. How did you store potatoes?  Pie 'em.
There's some taters to pie up in the end shed.
A few days after digging the carrots and other things have been pie'd.
Potatoes can be ‘pieing’ instead of burying them in the ground in the same way as turnips are.
She says he goes to pye potatoes.
Pie the old potatoes into a ditch by the wood-side.
As soon as they are raised out of the ground, they should be put into straw to ‘pye’, as it is called in Norfolk.
‘The old wight has been pieing it.’ ‘Pieing what?’ ‘I don't know 'ow he'd got to work, if th' old wight has been piein' t' potaters.’
He told me that most of it was in his hovel or ‘pied’ in the field.
Q. What do you say to potatoes when you cover them over after digging?  Pie, you pie 'em.
We pyed the potatoes to save them for later on.
A man who does that sort of thing is known as a pyer.
The first crop was pied at the end of July.

The word pie is used to indicate the storing of potatoes and vegetables in large earthenware vessels and sometimes to indicate that such storing takes place under ground in a pit or in a cellar where it has been filled with soil.
I's a-got to pie the potaties.
They had pied potatoes last night but she thought they were a bit too green yet.
They had been in the ground all summer. They were not pieing any more of it that season.
The potatoes in the garden were to be pie'd.
In winter they are usually ‘pieled’, which means that the crop is put in heaps and covered with straw, earth, or clay.
‘It's time I was pieing 'em.’ ‘Pie them?’ said Eddie. ‘It means putting 'em in the barn for winter, like.’

At harvest time the men were busily piering up their potatoes and digging their cabbages into ‘clamps’ to carry them home in sack load after load from the fields to be hung up in the kitchen and kept under cover till wanted for Christmas and for later on.
She put in a bit of potatoes 'n' pie 'em over.
They must be planted in the second week of May and ‘pied’ as soon as they are brought in.
It's the only way of keeping potatoes in the ground, you see, if they're pieed up at harvest time.
The tubers are then ‘pieing’—that is, stacked two-thirds deep in a straw pit (pie), covered over with straw and left to rot.
Pieing. A method of storing potatoes in straw-covered heaps which was very popular until about thirty years ago.
He pies 'em in a straw stooks with a coverin'.
Pie, to cover potatoes with straw and soil, for winter storage.
A few days later when the ground is frozen you will be able to dig these out of their straw or turf ‘beds’ and pie them again under straw in another bed.
I'm going to pye the spuds.
You have to dig it up then, and pie it again, and keep it snug.
‘There's 'e great pile 'a taters we're pyeing’.
Pieing, when potatoes were pitted to keep them warm.
In the winter they were taken out of the ground in the winter for ‘pyeing’, or storing away in earthen pits.
To ‘pie’ the crop into heaps covered with straw.
Pit it, and pie it.
Q. What does pieing potatoes mean?
He says: ‘If it's done the pying, they'll keep for months.’
They've pied their potatoes up, and they haven't done it in the right way.
In early days she said there were no deep freezers and so you pie potatoes for the winter.
At Christmas we got to pie potatoes and there were huge big wods to pie up.
When potatoes were not eaten during the season they had to be pyed up and stored underground.
That potato field—pying up taters for winter.
Q. What is the use of pieing the potatoes? A. To keep the potatoes warm when they are being dried.
Pots will keep over winter but only if you ‘pye’ them under straw.
I'll pie up the potatoes when they've cooked.
Pie the potatoes for the winter.
‘Pie’  the potatoes after they have been lifted, i.e. put them into a hill (a ‘pie’) covered over with straw.
Pieing potatoes is more important than picking them.
Pie, to heap potatoes in pits to be stored; also of potatoes, etc.
When a crop is pie'd it's put in earthen pit, covered with straw and sods. It's done about this time of year when the ground's pretty stiff, when it's not likely to turn and spoil the crop.
A pyeing house, built to cover potatoes for winter storage was used in the fields from about 1600 to 1650.
Q. What would you say if you were going to cover potatoes with straw and turn soil over them?  Pie 'em.
Pieing, putting vegetables such as potatoes and cabbages into a straw-lined pit for winter storage.
Pie, to pile or heap up, as in pieing potatoes for winter use.
I remember my father pyeing his potatoes under the potato-beds at the end of every summer to keep them warm through the winter.
